$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{({2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{2}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{e}^{t}]={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{t}{4}]={e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{[{e}^{t}]}^{2}+{[{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recognizing that the term under the square root is a perfect square, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}({e}^{3t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$  We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{e}^{t}]={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{t}{4}]={e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{[{e}^{t}]}^{2}+{[{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recognizing that the term under the square root is a perfect square, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}({e}^{3t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$  We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+\frac{u}{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{2}{4})-(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4})] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{7}{3}+\frac{1}{4}] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{28}{12}+\frac{3}{12}] \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{31}{12} \\  & =\frac{31\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-019c2510-13c6-5cb5-adc7-f6823183b11a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-019c2510-13c6-5cb5-adc7-f6823183b11a" :answer-field/id #uuid "019c2510-13c6-5cb5-adc7-f6823183b11a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-717f0fc3-0cb4-5e82-a464-045bfd255128" :answer-field/choices ["answer-717f0fc3-0cb4-5e82-a464-045bfd255128"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-717f0fc3-0cb4-5e82-a464-045bfd255128" :answer/id #uuid "717f0fc3-0cb4-5e82-a464-045bfd255128" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{31\pi}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d124471f-78aa-50f9-bfd3-0eadf2ea5bb7" :question/id #uuid "d124471f-78aa-50f9-bfd3-0eadf2ea5bb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-138972" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}={sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}),$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{0}-2(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi \cdot {[u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16\pi (1-\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{e}^{t}]={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{t}{4}]={e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{[{e}^{t}]}^{2}+{[{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\pi.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\sin^2 t +\cos^2 t= 1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{3}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049272} {:db/id 17592186050860} {:db/id 17592186129487 :question/id #uuid "2fe9bcdf-6522-538a-a529-97fa9381c2b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-138944"} {:db/id 17592186129493 $$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)=3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3/2})=3{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9(1+t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+t.$ Then, $1+3t=3u-2$ and $\textrm{d}u = \textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3u-2)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3{u}^{3/2}-2{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{6{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{4{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{6({2}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{4({2}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{24\sqrt{2}}{5}-\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{15}+\frac{2}{15}] \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{5}(16\sqrt{2}+1).\end{aligned}

$$
S =  \int 2\pi y \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

Now suppose we have a parametrically defined curve: 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t \in \left[t_1,t_2\right].
$$

In the case of a parametric curve, the arc length element $\textrm{d}s$ is given by

$$
\textrm{d}s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

As a result, we obtain the following formula for the surface area generated by rotating a parametrically defined curve about the $x$-axis:

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t
$$

 

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "36a57433-1c78-58b8-860c-0ea6e3471761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6113 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c5c27e9e-03cb-5a93-8a56-bd33588960fe" :step/math-academy-id 618749 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130301}} {:db/id 17592186130301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}, \qquad
t \in [0,\pi].
$$

If we rotate this curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we obtain a sphere of radius $1.$ 

![](images/d0/d0d323b764b70d3f2830d821636a9bc27b40e7f7e9f45df909c81dd279dc16e4.png)

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)=-\operatorname{sin}t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)=\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of our surface of revolution can be computed as follows:
